712181.t: From Proto-Hellenic *tú, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂. Cognates include Sanskrit त्वम् (tvam), Latin tū, Persian تو (to) and Old English þū (English thou).

712188.t: From συγγιγνώσκω (sŭngĭgnṓskō, “to agree with; to acknowledge; to excuse; to pardon”) + -μη (-mē); by surface analysis, συν- (sŭn-) + γνώμη (gnṓmē).

712179.t: Perhaps from some extension, likely *sth₂-u-lo-s, of Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”); compare στύω (stū́ō, “to make stiff”).

712185.t: From συν- (sŭn-, “with”) + the root of γίγνομαι (gígnomai, “to be born”) + -ής (-ḗs, adjectival suffix).

712152.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ster- Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃- Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Indo-European *str̥tós Proto-Hellenic *strətós Ancient Greek στρατός From Proto-Hellenic *strətós, from Proto-Indo-European *str̥tós, from *ster- (“to…

712120.t: From στέλλω (stéllō, “to clothe”) + -η (-ē). Compare deverbal English dress.

712146.t: From an unattested *στρατιάομαι (*stratiáomai) + -της (-tēs). Another analysis (ultimately from the same root) takes the word as a derivative in -ιώτης (-iṓtēs) of στρατός (stratós, “troop, department of the people”).

712167.t: The etymology remains highly uncertain, but Beekes suspects a Pre-Greek origin.

712113.t: From στείχω (steíkhō, “walk, march, go or come, march in line or order”), from Proto-Indo-European *steygʰ- (“to walk”). Cognate with German steigen, English sty, stair, stile and possibly Latin vestīgō.

712165.t: Of unclear origin. According to Frisk, an adjectival formation from the o-grade of στράγξ (stránx, “trickle, drop”) (as drops tend to be rounded), and/or with morphological influence from γογγύλος (gongŭ́los, “round, spherical”).

712114.t: From Proto-Hellenic *stōyyā́, from Proto-Indo-European *stoh₂-w-ih₂, ultimately from the root *steh₂- (“to stand”), whence also στῦλος (stûlos, “column, pillar”).

712124.t: From στέλλω (stéllō, “to send”) + -ος (-os). See also στολή (stolḗ).

712157.t: From στρέφω (stréphō, “to twist”) and the suffix -μα (-ma).

712160.t: The traditional Indo-European analysis reconstructed *strebʰ- (“to twist”) and compared it with Proto-West Germanic *stroppōn (“to twist, writhe”).

712106.t: Beekes concludes that this may be Pre-Greek based on the derivations with π instead of β.

712154.t: Maybe from Proto-Indo-European *strebʰ- (“to twist”), which στρέφω (stréphō, “to twist”) is also often derived from.

712178.t: From στυγέω (stugéō) + -νός (-nós), of uncertain origin, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewg- (“to hit, push”) (compare Sanskrit तुज् (tuj, “to push, drive”)).

712170.t: Ultimately from στρέφω (stréphō, “to turn; to rotate”).

712158.t: From στρέφω (stréphō, “I turn, I twist”) + -τός (-tós, “able to”).

712174.t: Perhaps from an adjective *στρωμνός (*strōmnós, “spread”) -ή (-ḗ), itself from στρῶμα (strôma).

712116.t: From στείβω (steíbō, “to tread, stamp”) + -η (-ē). The "cushion" and "padding" senses are from the custom of filling pillows and mattresses using shrub leaves.

712128.t: From Proto-Hellenic *stórnūmi, from Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃- (“to spread, extend”) via Proto-Indo-European *str̥néh₃ti. Likely related to Swedish strö (“spread, sprinkle”).

712199.t: From συν- (sŭn-, “with; together”) + καλέω (kăléō, “to call”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁-.

712171.t: From the o-grade of στρέφω (stréphō, “to twist, turn”) + -ος (-os).

712176.t: From Proto-Hellenic *stugéō, from Proto-Indo-European *stug-éyeti, from *(s)tewg- (“to push, hit”).
